<USER_REQUEST>
Yes. A MetaMotion-style IMU can be used as a gesture controller for a drone, but the key is to translate human wrist/arm orientation and movement into a small set of intentional flight commands rather than trying to directly mimic every aircraft movement.

A good architecture is:

MetaMotion → sensor fusion → gesture recognition → flight command → drone

5
1. What MetaMotion gives you

A MetaMotion/MetaMotionS-type wearable provides the important signals you need:

Sensor	What it measures	Useful for drone control
Accelerometer	Linear acceleration + gravity	Detect hand movement, thrust gestures
Gyroscope	Angular velocity	Detect wrist rotation / quick movements
Magnetometer	Magnetic heading	Absolute-ish heading / yaw reference
Sensor fusion	Orientation	Roll, pitch, yaw/orientation
BLE	Wireless data	Send commands to Python controller

The most useful derived values are:

Roll — hand tilted left/right
Pitch — hand tilted forward/back
Yaw — hand rotated clockwise/counterclockwise
Acceleration — deliberate hand movements
Angular velocity — quick wrist rotations
Gesture duration
Gesture magnitude
2. Map human hand motion to drone motion

Think of your hand as a virtual aircraft joystick.

Hand tilt forward → Drone moves forward
       Hand
        ↓
       / 
      /  forward tilt

              DRONE
                →
             Forward

For example:

Pitch forward 15° → drone forward

Pitch backward 15° → drone backward

Hand tilt left/right → Drone moves sideways
Hand tilted left

       \
        \
         \

Drone ←

Roll left 15° → drone moves left

Roll right 15° → drone moves right

Rotate wrist → Drone yaw
       ↻

   wrist rotation

        DRONE
          ↻

Yaw clockwise → rotate drone clockwise

Yaw counterclockwise → rotate drone counterclockwise

Raise/lower hand → altitude

This one is more difficult because an accelerometer cannot reliably tell you absolute hand height.

Instead, use a gesture:

Hand ↑↑  → Drone ascend

Hand ↓↓  → Drone descend

Detect this from acceleration over a short period rather than simply using accelerometer Z.

3. I would NOT use continuous control initially

This is very important.

Don't start with:

"Every tiny movement of the wrist controls the drone."

That can become dangerous and frustrating.

Instead use intentional gestures.

For example:

Gesture	Drone command
Hand tilt forward	Forward
Hand tilt backward	Backward
Hand tilt left	Left
Hand tilt right	Right
Wrist rotate clockwise	Yaw right
Wrist rotate counterclockwise	Yaw left
Hand raise	Up
Hand lower	Down
Quick forward flick	Move forward
Quick backward flick	Move backward
Double tap/shake	Special action
Hold steady	Hover
Palm/arm still for X sec	Hover
4. A very useful gesture vocabulary

For your project, I'd divide gestures into three categories.

A. Continuous gestures

These control the drone while the gesture is maintained.

1. Forward
Pitch > +10°

→ Forward

2. Backward
Pitch < -10°

→ Backward

3. Left
Roll < -10°

→ Left

4. Right
Roll > +10°

→ Right

5. Rotate left
Yaw velocity < threshold

→ Yaw left

6. Rotate right
Yaw velocity > threshold

→ Yaw right

7. Neutral
|pitch| < 5°
|roll| < 5°
angular velocity low

→ Hover

This is probably the simplest control model.

5. Discrete gestures

These are better for safety-critical commands.

For example:

Takeoff

Don't use "raise hand" alone.

Use:

Raise → hold → return to neutral

UP
 ↑
 ↑
 HOLD
 ↓
NEUTRAL

      ↓

TAKEOFF

Or a specific double gesture.

Landing

For example:

Down gesture
     ↓
Hold 1 sec
     ↓
LAND

This prevents accidental landing from a small wrist movement.

Emergency stop

A very distinctive gesture could be:

rapid wrist shake
← → ← →

→ emergency hover/stop.

However, for a real drone, I would not rely exclusively on the wearable for emergency stopping. The drone's normal failsafe/controller should remain available.

6. Sensor fusion is the important part

The raw accelerometer isn't enough.

You want something like:

Accelerometer ─┐
               │
Gyroscope ─────┼──> Sensor Fusion ──> Orientation
               │
Magnetometer ──┘
                         │
                         ├── Roll
                         ├── Pitch
                         └── Yaw

You can use:

Madgwick filter
Mahony filter
Kalman filter
complementary filter

For your Python prototype, Madgwick is a particularly good starting point.

7. Gesture recognition pipeline

I'd build your Python system like this:

             MetaMotion
                  │
                  ▼
             BLE packets
                  │
                  ▼
          Sensor preprocessing
                  │
          ┌───────┴───────┐
          ▼               ▼
     Accelerometer      Gyro
          │               │
          └───────┬───────┘
                  ▼
             Sensor Fusion
                  │
                  ▼
           Roll/Pitch/Yaw
                  │
                  ▼
          Gesture Detector
                  │
                  ▼
       ┌─────────────────────┐
       │ Gesture → Drone Cmd  │
       └─────────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
           Drone SDK/API
                  │
                  ▼
                DRONE
8. Use a state machine

This will make your system much more reliable than simply doing:

if pitch > 10:
    forward()

Instead:

IDLE
 │
 │ activation gesture
 ▼
ARMED
 │
 ├── forward gesture → FORWARD
 ├── backward gesture → BACKWARD
 ├── left gesture → LEFT
 ├── right gesture → RIGHT
 ├── rotate gesture → YAW
 ├── up gesture → ASCEND
 ├── down gesture → DESCEND
 │
 ▼
HOVER

And importantly:

No valid gesture
       ↓
     HOVER

That gives you a fail-neutral design.

9. Add calibration

Every person's wrist position will be different.

When the system starts:

"Hold your hand in neutral position"

        ↓

Collect 2–3 seconds

        ↓

Calculate:
baseline_roll
baseline_pitch
baseline_yaw

        ↓

Use deviations from baseline

Then:

relative_pitch = pitch - neutral_pitch
relative_roll  = roll - neutral_roll

This is much better than assuming everyone holds the MetaMotion at exactly the same angle.

10. Dead zone is essential

Suppose neutral wrist orientation is:

pitch = 0°
roll  = 0°

Don't make 1° movement mean something.

Use:

-5° to +5° → HOVER

Then:

+5° to +15° → slow movement
+15° to +30° → medium movement
>30°        → maximum

For example:

Pitch

  +30° ───────── Maximum Forward
  +20° ───────── Fast Forward
  +10° ───────── Slow Forward
   +5° ───────── Dead zone
    0° ───────── Neutral
   -5° ───────── Dead zone
  -10° ───────── Slow Backward
  -20° ───────── Fast Backward
  -30° ───────── Maximum Backward

This gives you proportional control.

11. Even better: gesture confidence

Instead of:

gesture = FORWARD

your recognition layer can produce:

{
    "gesture": "FORWARD",
    "confidence": 0.92,
    "duration": 0.48,
    "magnitude": 18.5
}

Then your drone controller can say:

confidence > 0.8
       ↓
execute

confidence < 0.8
       ↓
hover

This is especially useful if you're eventually combining the wearable with your Python/Pygame movement-based game work.

12. Interesting advanced gestures

Once basic control works, you can recognize motion patterns.

Flick
neutral
   ↓
rapid forward acceleration
   ↓
return to neutral

→ short forward movement

Circle
      ↑
   ↗     ↘
  ←       →
   ↖     ↙
      ↓

→ drone orbit/rotation command

Double flick
→ ← → ←

→ special command

Wrist twist
↻

→ yaw

Hold
orientation unchanged for > 1 sec

→ continue current command

Freeze
sudden movement → neutral

→ hover

13. One important limitation

A MetaMotion IMU cannot directly know the absolute position of your hand.

For example:

"Move my hand 2 feet upward"

is difficult to determine accurately using only accelerometer + gyro + magnetometer because integrating acceleration twice to estimate position causes drift.

So:

Orientation gestures = excellent

Relative motion gestures = good

Absolute position tracking = poor

If you eventually want true 3D hand position, you would combine the IMU with something such as:

computer vision
UWB
optical tracking
depth camera
external positioning system
14. My recommended first version

I would start with only 7 commands:

             META MOTION
                  │
       ┌──────────┴──────────┐
       │                     │
    Orientation           Motion
       │                     │
       ▼                     ▼
 Forward / Back         Up / Down
 Left / Right
 Yaw Left / Right
       │
       ▼
     HOVER

Specifically:

MetaMotion gesture	Drone
Neutral	Hover
Tilt forward	Forward
Tilt backward	Backward
Tilt left	Strafe left
Tilt right	Strafe right
Rotate wrist left	Yaw left
Rotate wrist right	Yaw right
Raise hand	Ascend
Lower hand	Descend
Special confirmed gesture	Takeoff
Special confirmed gesture	Land

That is enough to build a first working prototype.

Recommended development sequence

Phase 1: MetaMotion → Python → display Roll/Pitch/Yaw on screen.

Phase 2: Roll/Pitch/Yaw → recognize gestures.

Phase 3: Gesture → virtual drone in Pygame.

Phase 4: Virtual drone → real drone SDK.

Phase 5: Add calibration, dead zones, confidence, smoothing and failsafes.

Phase 6: Add ML-based gesture recognition if you need more complex gestures.

If your goal is specifically to build this with MetaMotionS + Python, 
I can next give you a concrete MetaMotion → Python BLE → sensor-fusion → gesture-recognition architecture, including the Python classes and the exact accelerometer/gyro thresholds to start experimenting with.

how these gestures can be mapped to cerebral palsy kid when meta motions device attached to his wrist - his condition is Movement issues: Stiff muscles (spasticity), uncontrolled movements, or poor balance and coordination.

Yes — and this changes the design quite a lot.

For a child with cerebral palsy who has spasticity, involuntary movements, and reduced coordination, I would not take the normal drone-controller model of “tilt 10° = move drone” and apply it directly. The system should learn the child's intentional movement relative to their own baseline, rather than expecting a precise movement.

This is actually a promising use of an IMU: studies have used wrist-worn inertial sensors in children with CP to measure upper-limb activity, asymmetry, movement quality, and movement characteristics. IMU-derived measures can capture features such as acceleration, angular velocity, and movement smoothness.

The key idea: don't recognize "perfect gestures"

Instead of asking:

"Did the child tilt their wrist exactly 15° forward?"

ask:

"Did the child's movement show enough evidence of an intentional forward movement?"

That distinction is extremely important.

For example, if the child's wrist naturally sits at:

+25° pitch

and they can intentionally move it to:

+32°

that 7° movement may be meaningful for that child.

Another child might naturally sit at 0° and comfortably move 20°.

So your system should be personalized per child.

1. Change the drone-control model

For a typical person:

Wrist angle
     ↓
Drone command

For a child with CP:

Wrist sensor
     ↓
Individual baseline
     ↓
Movement filtering
     ↓
Intentional movement detection
     ↓
Gesture confidence
     ↓
Drone/game command

This is much safer and much more accessible.

2. Don't use absolute wrist position

Suppose the child's wrist is naturally:

Pitch = +22°
Roll  = -8°

Don't interpret that as:

"The child is commanding the drone forward."

Instead, during calibration:

Child's comfortable position

Pitch = +22°
Roll  = -8°

       ↓

Store as NEUTRAL

Then look at changes:

Current pitch = +29°

29 - 22 = +7°

        ↓

Intentional forward movement?

This makes the system much more tolerant of spasticity and abnormal resting posture.

3. I would use very large "movement zones"

Instead of requiring precise gestures:

Forward
Small movement
     ↓
   +3°
   +5°
   +7°
     ↓
FORWARD INTENT
Backward
-3°
-5°
-7°
     ↓
BACKWARD INTENT

The actual thresholds should be calibrated individually, not hard-coded.

A published CP rehabilitation approach using MetaMotion IMUs similarly describes individualized intensity thresholds based on each participant's maximum movement capability rather than one universal threshold.

4. Use acceleration + gyro, not just orientation

This is probably the biggest improvement I'd make to your design.

Suppose the child's hand has involuntary shaking:

← → ← → ← → 

If you only look at orientation, you might incorrectly detect:

LEFT
RIGHT
LEFT
RIGHT

Instead, combine:

Accelerometer

"What movement occurred?"

Gyroscope

"Did the wrist actually rotate?"

Orientation

"Which direction did the movement occur?"

Timing

"Was it sustained long enough to be intentional?"

Then:

                 MetaMotion
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        ↓            ↓            ↓
      Accel         Gyro      Orientation
        │            │            │
        └────────────┼────────────┘
                     ↓
              Movement filter
                     ↓
             Intent classifier
                     ↓
              Drone command

IMUs are particularly useful for CP because accelerometers and gyroscopes can capture linear acceleration, angular velocity, and abnormal movement characteristics. Research has specifically found differences in acceleration/angular velocity and other movement parameters in dyskinetic CP.

5. Separate "intentional movement" from "involuntary movement"

This is the heart of your project.

Imagine the sensor produces:

Time →

Accel
  │
  │    /\        /\ /\       /\
  │   /  \  /\  /  V \  /\ /  \
  │__/____\/__\/______\/__\/____

Some of those movements are involuntary.

You want to detect:

     INTENTIONAL
         ↓
       /────\
      /      \
_____/        \________

rather than reacting to every spike.

Useful features include:

movement amplitude
duration
acceleration
angular velocity
direction consistency
smoothness
repetition
time spent in a movement
return-to-neutral behavior
signal variability

Movement smoothness and related sensor-derived features have already been investigated as indicators of motor capacity in children with CP.

6. Don't make the child "hold" a precise position

For a child with spasticity, this could be frustrating.

Instead of:

Hold wrist at +15° for 2 seconds.

use:

Move approximately forward.

For example:

             Forward zone

          +++++++++++++++++
          +               +
          +    MOVE       +
          +   FORWARD     +
          +               +
          +++++++++++++++++

             Neutral

Once the sensor sees sufficient forward movement:

DRONE → FORWARD

The child doesn't need to be precise.

7. Use "effort-based" control

This could be especially good for your game.

Instead of:

10° = Forward
20° = Faster Forward
30° = Very Fast

use:

Child's minimum intentional movement
             ↓
        30% effort
             ↓
        Slow drone

Child's stronger movement
             ↓
        60% effort
             ↓
        Medium drone

Child's maximum comfortable movement
             ↓
        100% effort
             ↓
        Fast drone

This turns the system into an adaptive controller.

8. Example for one child

Suppose during calibration the child can comfortably produce:

Forward movement:
minimum detectable = 5°
maximum comfortable = 18°

Right:
minimum detectable = 4°
maximum comfortable = 15°

Left:
minimum detectable = 3°
maximum comfortable = 12°

The software automatically creates:

FORWARD

<5°       → ignore
5–9°      → slow
9–14°     → medium
14–18°    → fast
>18°      → cap at maximum

Notice that 18° is not required.

The child can participate even with a 5° movement.

9. Very important: don't use "shake" as an emergency gesture

My previous suggestion of wrist shaking for emergency control would not be appropriate here.

A child with uncontrolled movement could accidentally trigger it.

Instead:

Normal movement → game command

Uncertain movement → NO COMMAND

Communication lost → HOVER

Sensor abnormality → HOVER

Emergency → independent drone failsafe

That's much safer.

10. I would actually simplify the gestures

For this use case, I wouldn't start with 10–15 gestures.

I'd use four directional gestures:

Child's movement	Game/drone
Move wrist forward	Drone forward
Move wrist backward	Drone backward
Move wrist left	Drone left
Move wrist right	Drone right

Then use separate game actions for:

Action	Possible gesture
Start	intentional double movement
Stop	return to neutral + hold
Takeoff	sustained upward/forward gesture
Landing	sustained downward gesture

But I'd initially implement these in a virtual drone, not a physical drone.

11. You can make the system forgiving

This is where your game can become really interesting.

Suppose the child attempts:

FORWARD

but produces:

forward + slight left + involuntary shake

Don't say:

Invalid gesture.

Instead:

             Movement
                ↓
        ┌───────────────┐
        │  72% FORWARD  │
        │  18% LEFT     │
        │  10% NOISE    │
        └───────────────┘
                ↓
          FORWARD

The game rewards intent, not precision.

12. Add a confidence score

This would be excellent for your Python implementation.

For example:

Forward confidence = 0.87

Left confidence = 0.21

Involuntary/noise = 0.18

Then:

if forward_confidence > 0.70:
    drone.forward()
else:
    drone.hover()

You could even have:

0.00–0.40 → ignore
0.40–0.70 → slow movement
0.70–0.85 → normal movement
0.85–1.00 → strong movement

Again, these are starting values, not clinical thresholds.

13. Calibration should become part of the game

This is something I particularly recommend for your project.

Don't make calibration feel like a medical test.

Make it a fun game.

Game: "Wake up the drone"

Screen:

🚁 Let's wake up your drone!

Then:

"Move your hand forward!"

Child attempts movement.

Drone moves a little.

⭐ Great!

Then:

"Move left!"

Drone moves.

Then:

"Move right!"

Then:

"Move backward!"

The system learns:

Srihari's movement profile

Forward:  ███████░░
Backward: █████░░░░
Left:     ████░░░░░
Right:    ██████░░░
Noise:    ██░░░░░░░

The game now knows his movement, rather than assuming a typical child's movement.

14. You can even turn involuntary movement into something useful

Don't necessarily treat all extra movement as "bad."

For example:

Intentional movement
        +
Movement quality
        +
Consistency

can control different game mechanics.

For example:

Smooth movement → drone flies smoothly

Strong intentional movement → drone accelerates

Repeated movement → collect coins

Hold steady → hover and collect target

This could turn therapy-like movement into gameplay.

15. Your earlier music idea fits extremely well

You mentioned wanting BGM and encouraging lyrics for the game.

You could connect movement quality to the music:

Child movement
      ↓
Gesture recognition
      ↓
Game event
      ↓
Music response

For example:

Forward movement

🎵 "Go, go, go!"

Successful left movement

🎵 "Great job!"

Smooth movement

🥁 Add drum beat

Repeated successful movements

🎶 Add another musical layer

Mission completed

🎵 Personalized celebration/song

This approach has precedent in rehabilitation research: a recent CP trial using MetaMotion IMUs describes converting accelerometer/gyroscope signals into commands and providing real-time auditory feedback based on individualized movement-intensity thresholds.

16. One MetaMotion vs two MetaMotions

If your goal is simply controlling the game/drone, one wrist sensor is a good starting point.

If your goal becomes measuring improvement, two sensors become much more interesting.

       Left wrist              Right wrist
           │                       │
        IMU #1                  IMU #2
           │                       │
           └──────────┬────────────┘
                      ↓
             Compare movement
                      ↓
             Symmetry / usage

For unilateral CP, comparing affected and unaffected arm activity is a commonly studied approach with wrist-worn sensors.

That could let your system distinguish:

"The child moved."

from:

"The child is increasingly using the affected arm."

That's potentially much more valuable for a rehabilitation-oriented game.

17. The architecture I'd recommend for your project

Given that you're already working with Python + MetaMotion + a movement-based game, I'd build it like this:

              META MOTION
                   │
          Accelerometer
          Gyroscope
          Magnetometer
                   │
                   ▼
          ┌────────────────┐
          │ Sensor Fusion  │
          └────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼
          ┌────────────────┐
          │ Child Profile  │
          │ Calibration    │
          └────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼
          ┌────────────────┐
          │ Noise Filter   │
          │ + Smoothing    │
          └────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼
          ┌────────────────┐
          │ Intent Detector│
          └────────────────┘
                   │
          ┌────────┼─────────┐
          ▼        ▼         ▼
       Forward    Left     Right
       Backward   etc.     etc.
          │        │         │
          └────────┼─────────┘
                   ▼
             PYGAME DRONE
                   │
          ┌────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                  ▼
       Visual              Music
       Feedback             Feedback
And the most important principle:

Don't build a "drone controller for a child with CP."

Build a personalized movement-intent controller that happens to control a drone/game.

That makes your design much more tolerant of spasticity, involuntary movement, and poor coordination. It also aligns better with the emerging use of wearable IMUs for personalized movement assessment and rehabilitation in CP.

For a real child and especially a physical drone, this should be treated as an assistive/experimental system and tested with the child's PT/OT and appropriate safety controls; the sensor should never be the sole safety mechanism.

If you want, the next useful step is to 
design the actual MetaMotion algorithm for Srihari: calibration → filtering → involuntary-motion rejection → 4 gesture detection → confidence score → Pygame drone movement, with Python pseudocode and recommended starting thresholds.

what gestures we need to detect from meta motions for scratch pad with sketching draw lines, for normal kids and cerebral palsy kids - drone gestures and sketch gestures for bothe normal and accessible mode as prompt

Yes. I would design two gesture profiles—Normal Mode and Accessible Mode—but keep the underlying MetaMotion sensor pipeline the same. The Accessible Mode should recognize intentional movement, tolerate spasticity/uncontrolled motion, and require less precision.

Here is a consolidated prompt you can use for designing the system.

MetaMotion Gesture-Controlled Scratch Pad and Drone

Design a Python-based interactive game controller using a MetaMotion/MetaMotionS wearable IMU attached to the player's wrist.

The system must support two modes:

Normal Mode — optimized for children with typical motor control.
Accessible Mode — optimized for children with cerebral palsy or other movement/coordination difficulties, including spasticity, involuntary movements, limited range of motion, and reduced coordination.

The system should never assume that every player can perform the same movement amplitude. Accessible Mode must be personalized through calibration.

1. Sensor Inputs

Use MetaMotion sensor data:

Accelerometer
Gyroscope
Magnetometer, when useful
Sensor-fusion orientation
Roll
Pitch
Yaw
Angular velocity
Linear acceleration
Movement duration
Movement amplitude
Movement consistency
Movement smoothness

Process the raw signals using filtering and sensor fusion before gesture recognition.

Use a short calibration period to determine each player's natural wrist position and comfortable movement range.

2. Scratch Pad / Sketching Mode

The player controls a virtual drawing cursor using wrist movements.

Normal Mode — Drawing Gestures
Cursor movement
Wrist gesture	Drawing action
Tilt wrist forward	Move cursor up
Tilt wrist backward	Move cursor down
Tilt wrist left	Move cursor left
Tilt wrist right	Move cursor right
Hold neutral	Stop cursor
Slow wrist movement	Slow cursor
Larger wrist movement	Faster cursor
Drawing

Use a deliberate forward/hold gesture to activate the drawing pen.

Neutral → intentional movement → DRAW

The cursor should draw a continuous line while the drawing gesture remains active.

Pen Up / Stop Drawing

Return to neutral and hold briefly.

Movement → DRAW
Neutral → PEN UP
Additional gestures
Gesture	Action
Quick forward flick	Start a short stroke
Quick backward flick	Undo last stroke
Small clockwise wrist rotation	Rotate brush/tool
Small counterclockwise rotation	Change brush/tool
Double intentional movement	Clear/erase mode
Hold steady	Pause drawing

Avoid requiring very precise wrist angles.

3. Accessible Mode — Scratch Pad

Accessible Mode must NOT require the child to reproduce a perfect drawing gesture.

The system should recognize movement intention rather than exact wrist orientation.

First perform calibration:

"Hold your hand comfortably."

Record:
neutral_roll
neutral_pitch
neutral_yaw
movement_range
movement_noise
movement_speed

Determine the child's comfortable minimum and maximum movement for each direction.

Example:

Forward:
minimum intentional movement = 5°
maximum comfortable movement = 15°

Left:
minimum intentional movement = 4°
maximum comfortable movement = 12°

Do not use universal thresholds.

Accessible Drawing Gestures
Move cursor

Detect intentional directional movement:

Forward intent  → cursor up
Backward intent → cursor down
Left intent     → cursor left
Right intent    → cursor right

The movement does NOT need to be perfectly straight.

If the movement is:

Forward + small left deviation

interpret it primarily as:

FORWARD

rather than rejecting the gesture.

Adaptive Cursor

Implement:

small intentional movement
        ↓
small cursor movement

medium intentional movement
        ↓
medium cursor movement

large comfortable movement
        ↓
larger cursor movement

Never require the child to reach a maximum angle.

Accessible Drawing Activation

Provide multiple ways to activate drawing.

Preferred:

Intentional movement → DRAW

Alternative:

Hold wrist reasonably steady for ~0.5–1 second
        ↓
PEN DOWN

The child should not need to perform a complicated gesture.

Spasticity / Involuntary Movement Handling

Do not interpret every accelerometer spike as a gesture.

Use:

Low-pass filtering
Moving average
Median filtering
Gyroscope confirmation
Movement duration
Direction consistency
Minimum movement duration
Hysteresis
Dead zones
Gesture confidence
Personalized thresholds

Example:

Sensor movement
      ↓
Is movement above child's intentional threshold?
      ↓
YES
      ↓
Is direction reasonably consistent?
      ↓
YES
      ↓
Intentional gesture

If confidence is low:

LOW CONFIDENCE → NO ACTION

Do not punish the child for involuntary movement.

4. Drawing Modes

Support several accessible drawing modes.

Free Draw

Wrist movement directly controls the cursor.

Move → Draw
Assisted Draw

Smooth the cursor path automatically.

Raw wrist path
      ↓
Smoothing
      ↓
Clean drawing
Shape Assist

If the child attempts a shape, automatically stabilize it.

Support:

Straight line
Circle
Square
Triangle
Arc

For example:

Child draws approximate line
          ↓
System recognizes line
          ↓
Straighten line

This allows children with limited motor control to create successful drawings.

Snap-to-Path

Provide optional targets:

Start ●────────────● End

The child only needs to move approximately toward the target.

5. Scratch Pad Feedback

Provide immediate positive feedback.

Examples:

"Great line!"
"Nice movement!"
"You did it!"
Stars
Coins
Animated trails
Sound effects
Musical notes

Do not evaluate drawing quality negatively.

Reward:

Attempt
Direction
Completion
Repetition
Increased movement
Smooth movement
6. Drone Control — Normal Mode

Use the wrist as a virtual drone controller.

Wrist gesture	Drone action
Tilt forward	Fly forward
Tilt backward	Fly backward
Tilt left	Fly/strafe left
Tilt right	Fly/strafe right
Rotate wrist clockwise	Yaw right
Rotate wrist counterclockwise	Yaw left
Raise hand	Ascend
Lower hand	Descend
Neutral	Hover

Use proportional control:

Small tilt → slow movement
Medium tilt → medium movement
Large tilt → faster movement
7. Drone Control — Accessible Mode

Do not require precise orientation.

Use personalized intentional movement detection.

Basic controls
Intentional forward movement
        ↓
Drone moves forward
Intentional backward movement
        ↓
Drone moves backward
Intentional left movement
        ↓
Drone moves left
Intentional right movement
        ↓
Drone moves right

If yaw control is difficult, make yaw optional.

If vertical movement is difficult, use automatic altitude holding.

8. Accessible Drone Assistance

Add automatic stabilization.

The child provides the direction; the software handles the difficult parts.

For example:

Child:
FORWARD

System:
maintain altitude
maintain orientation
limit speed
smooth acceleration
smooth deceleration

This produces:

Child controls INTENT
        +
Software controls STABILITY

This is preferable to requiring the child to control every drone axis simultaneously.

9. Drone Gesture Safety

Never use uncontrolled movement as a dangerous command.

Avoid:

Shake = emergency
Random movement = landing
Single accidental spike = takeoff

Use confirmation for critical commands.

Takeoff
Intentional gesture
      ↓
Confirmation
      ↓
TAKEOFF
Landing
Intentional landing gesture
      ↓
Hold/confirm
      ↓
LAND

For physical drones, retain an independent hardware/software failsafe and do not rely solely on the wearable.

During development, use a simulated drone first.

10. Gesture Confidence Model

Every detected gesture should produce:

{
    "gesture": "FORWARD",
    "confidence": 0.87,
    "amplitude": 0.62,
    "duration": 0.48,
    "smoothness": 0.71
}

Example:

confidence > 0.75
        ↓
execute command

confidence 0.40–0.75
        ↓
reduced/smoothed command

confidence < 0.40
        ↓
ignore

Thresholds must be configurable per child.

11. Common Gesture Layer

Build one common gesture-recognition engine:

                   MetaMotion
                       │
                       ▼
                Sensor Processing
                       │
                       ▼
                 Sensor Fusion
                       │
                       ▼
             Personalized Calibration
                       │
                       ▼
              Gesture Recognition
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │
        NORMAL MODE       ACCESSIBLE MODE
              │                 │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       ▼
              Application Commands
                  /           \
                 /             \
          Scratch Pad          Drone

The difference between modes should primarily be:

Thresholds
Filtering
Gesture tolerance
Assistance
Cursor/drone stabilization
Confidence requirements
Calibration

Do NOT create an entirely separate sensor system for Accessible Mode.

12. Important Accessible Design Principle

The system should recognize:

"The child intended to move right."

rather than:

"The child's wrist reached exactly +15 degrees roll."

This allows the same game to work for children with very different movement abilities.

13. Recommended First Gesture Set

Start with only these gestures.

Scratch Pad
FORWARD
BACKWARD
LEFT
RIGHT
DRAW
PEN UP
PAUSE
UNDO
Drone
FORWARD
BACKWARD
LEFT
RIGHT
YAW LEFT
YAW RIGHT
ASCEND
DESCEND
HOVER
TAKEOFF
LAND

Do not implement complicated gestures until these are reliable.

14. Final Product Goal

Create a playful movement-controlled system where:

NORMAL CHILD
     ↓
Precise wrist movement
     ↓
Direct control


CHILD WITH MOTOR DIFFICULTY
     ↓
Small intentional movement
     ↓
Adaptive recognition
     ↓
Assistance + stabilization
     ↓
Successful control

The goal is not to make the child adapt to the controller.

The controller should adapt to the child.

The system should maximize:

Participation
Successful attempts
Independence
Fun
Encouragement
Movement opportunity
Personalization

while minimizing:

Frustration
Required precision
False commands
Effects of involuntary movements
Fatigue
Complex gestures

A particularly strong implementation would make Scratch Pad and Drone use the same four fundamental movement primitives—forward, backward, left, right. Then the child learns one movement vocabulary, and you can reuse it across drawing, flying, collecting objects, racing, and other games. - plan

# MetaMotion Gesture-Controlled Scratch Pad and Drone Implementation Plan

This document outlines the architecture and plan to implement the MetaMotion-based interactive gesture controller, specifically adding a new Scratch Pad game and a Drone simulation (which could later bridge to a real drone), with support for both Normal and Accessible (cerebral palsy) modes.

## Background Context
The system uses a MetaMotion wearable IMU. Currently, the architecture supports games (like bricks, snake, fruit_ninja) via a gesture processing thread (`shared/gesture.py` and `shared/fusion_processor.py`). We need to introduce a new gesture vocabulary, personalized calibration, and intent-based filtering for an Accessible mode tailored to children with motor difficulties.

## User Review Required

> [!WARNING]  
> **Accessible Mode Intent Recognition vs. Current System**
> The current gesture system (`shared/gesture.py`) exports fixed values and thresholds (e.g., `tilt_y`). To support personalized Accessible mode, we need to introduce a calibration phase and a confidence-based gesture state. This requires modifying `shared/gesture.py` and `GestureState` to expose raw intent/confidence metrics alongside traditional thresholds. Are you comfortable with modifying the core `GestureState` to include confidence scores?

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Game Selection**
> We will create two new games in the `games/` folder: `scratch_pad` and `drone_sim`. These will need to be added to `home.py`. Should the Accessible/Normal mode toggle be globally managed in `home.py` (affecting all games) or per-game?

## Open Questions

1. **Calibration Flow:** Should calibration be a standalone "game/activity" (e.g., `games/calibration`), or a mandatory pre-game step that runs before starting *Scratch Pad* or *Drone*?
2. **Accessible Configuration:** Where should the personalized calibration data (comfortable movement ranges, noise profiles) be stored? Should it be saved to `data/profiles/{username}/accessible_profile.json`?
3. **Drone Sim vs Real Drone:** For phase 1, is it sufficient to build a purely visual Pygame drone simulation in `games/drone_sim/game.py`, similar to `rc_simulator.py`?

## Proposed Changes

### Core Sensor and Gesture Pipeline

We will enhance the existing gesture pipeline to support calibration and confidence-based intent detection.

#### [MODIFY] [`shared/gesture.py`](file:///Users/jerold/dev/Bricks/shared/gesture.py)
- **Add Calibration State:** Introduce logic to capture baseline orientation and movement ranges during a calibration phase.
- **Implement Noise Filtering:** Add low-pass filtering and moving averages for spasticity/involuntary movement handling.
- **Confidence Scoring:** Update the gesture state to include `gesture_confidence`, outputting a dictionary like `{"gesture": "FORWARD", "confidence": 0.85}` based on the user's calibrated baseline rather than absolute angles.

#### [MODIFY] [`shared/username_screen.py`](file:///Users/jerold/dev/Bricks/shared/username_screen.py) (or related profile code)
- **Add Mode Selection:** Add UI/logic to select between Normal Mode and Accessible Mode when choosing or creating a profile. Store this preference in the user's profile.

### New Games

We will implement the Scratch Pad and Drone Simulation as new Pygame modules.

#### [NEW] [`games/scratch_pad/game.py`](file:///Users/jerold/dev/Bricks/games/scratch_pad/game.py)
- **Virtual Cursor:** Implement a Pygame interface with a drawing canvas.
- **Normal Mode:** Map precise orientation (pitch/roll) to cursor movement. Deliberate forward movement activates drawing.
- **Accessible Mode:** Map directional *intent* (confidence > threshold) to smoothed cursor movement. Implement adaptive cursor speeds based on effort.
- **Features:** Free draw, pause, clear screen (via double intent). Provide rich visual and audio feedback.

#### [NEW] [`games/drone_sim/game.py`](file:///Users/jerold/dev/Bricks/games/drone_sim/game.py)
- **Drone UI:** Create a Pygame visualizer showing drone position, altitude, and orientation.
- **Normal Mode:** Full proportional control using wrist tilt for pitch/roll and wrist rotation for yaw.
- **Accessible Mode:** Simplified directional intent commands. Automatic stabilization and altitude holding.
- **Failsafes:** Implement hover-on-low-confidence logic and explicit confirmation for takeoff/landing.

#### [MODIFY] [`home.py`](file:///Users/jerold/dev/Bricks/home.py)
- Add "Scratch Pad" and "Drone Simulator" to the carousel of available games.
- Ensure the selected Accessibility mode is passed down to the games.

## Verification Plan

### Automated Tests
- If applicable, write basic logic tests for the confidence scoring algorithm to ensure involuntary spikes do not trigger high-confidence gestures. (e.g. `tests/test_gesture_confidence.py`).

### Manual Verification
1. Run the system and select Normal Mode.
2. Verify `Scratch Pad` cursor responds accurately to 1:1 wrist movements.
3. Verify `Drone Sim` responds proportionally to tilt.
4. Restart and select Accessible Mode.
5. Complete calibration (intentionally simulating restricted movement).
6. Verify that small intentional movements trigger commands, while simulated tremors/spasticity are filtered out.
7. Verify drawing stabilization (straightening) in Scratch Pad.

21:   Wrist twist CW  (gz positive)               →  CURVE RIGHT (ball spin)
22:   Wrist twist CCW (gz negative)               →  CURVE LEFT  (ball spin)
23: 
24:   Wrist tilted FORWARD → tilt_y < -tilt_threshold → UP (Snake)
25:   Wrist tilted BACK    → tilt_y > +tilt_threshold → DOWN (Snake)
26: 
27: All thresholds are adjustable via the GestureConfig dataclass.
28: """
29:

31: import time
32: import queue
33: import threading
34: import math
35: from collections import deque
36: from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace
37: from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

46: # ── Configuration ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
47: 
48: @dataclass
49: class GestureConfig:
50:     # Tilt dead-zone in g (calibration-relative lateral gravity shift).
51:     # ~0.05 g ≈ 3° of tilt — keeps paddle still when wrist is approximately flat.
52:     tilt_threshold: float = 0.05
53: 
54:     # Tilt value (g) at which paddle reaches full speed.
55:     # 0.5 g ≈ 30° of tilt — comfortable range for fast play.
56:     tilt_max: float = 0.5
57: 
58:     # Gyroscope flick threshold (°/s) to trigger a LAUNCH event.
59:     # 200°/s catches a firm-but-normal wrist flick; 300 was too high in practice.
60:     flick_threshold: float = 200.0
61: 
62:     # Low-pass smoothing factor for gravity extraction [0–1].
63:     # Lower = heavier filtering = slower response but motion-noise immune.
64:     # 0.05 at 100 Hz ≈ 2 Hz cutoff: tracks slow tilts, ignores quick shakes.
65:     alpha: float = 0.05
66: 
67:     # Number of samples in the rolling window used for flick detection.
68:     # 6 samples = 60ms at 100Hz — catches shorter/sharper flicks (was 80ms).
69:     flick_window: int = 6
70: 
71:     # Dead-zone for gyro twist (°/s).
72:     twist_dead_zone: float = 30.0
73: 
74:     # Time (s) between repeated LAUNCH events to prevent accidental double-fire.
75:     launch_cooldown: float = 0.4
76: 
77:     # Samples collected for auto-calibration (≈1 s at 100 Hz).
78:     # Keep sensor still during this period.
79:     calibration_samples: int = 100
80: 
81:     # Minimum seconds between gesture triggers on each axis.
82:     # Used by game modules in accessible mode; GestureInterpreter ignores it.
83:     gesture_cooldown: float = 0.8
84: 
85:     # Functional alignment angle (radians).
86:     # Compensates for sensor being mounted twisted on the wrist or contractures in the arm.
87:     yaw_offset_rads: float = 0.0
88: 
89:     # Gyroscope magnitude (°/s) below which the adaptive baseline is allowed to
90:     # drift toward the current resting gravity vector.  Prevents adaptation during
91:     # active gestures while accommodating slow tremors.
92:     gyro_adapt_threshold: float = 45.0
93: 
94:     # Rate at which the adaptive baseline is dragged toward the current resting
95:     # gravity vector each sample.  0.002 at 100 Hz ≈ 5 s to fully adapt.
96:     adapt_rate: float = 0.002
97: 
98:     # Duration (seconds) of the functional-calibration data-collection window.
99:     # The user performs a natural arm swing for this long; PCA finds the axis.
100:     functional_cal_seconds: float = 2.5
101: 
102:     # Flick-to-steer mode (for Snake)
103:     flick_steer_enabled: bool = False
104:     flick_steer_threshold: float = 160.0  # °/s, lower than launch flick
105:     flick_steer_cooldown: float = 0.5     # seconds between directional flicks
106:     flick_steer_window: int = 7           # samples to check for peak
107: 
108: 
109: # Pre-defined configs for different game modes.
110: # The main application can select which config to pass to the GestureInterpreter.
111: 
112: CONFIG_STANDARD = GestureConfig()
113: 
114: # ASTRA / Accessible mode: lower thresholds, longer cooldowns, and disabled spin
115: # make the game more forgiving for users with movement disabilities.
116: CONFIG_ACCESSIBLE = GestureConfig(
117:     tilt_threshold=0.04,      # More sensitive to small tilts
118:     tilt_max=0.4,             # Reach full speed with less effort
119:     flick_threshold=120.0,    # Lower flick threshold for launching
120:     twist_dead_zone=999.0,    # Effectively disables ball spin control
121:     launch_cooldown=1.0,      # Longer cooldown to prevent accidental double-launches
122:     gesture_cooldown=1.2,
123: )
124: 
125: # Variant of accessible mode for Snake that uses discrete flicks to turn.
126: CONFIG_ACCESSIBLE_FLICK_STEER = replace(
127:     CONFIG_ACCESSIBLE,
128:     flick_steer_enabled=True
129: )

131: # ── Gesture state ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

133: @dataclass
134: class GestureState:
135:     """
136:     Published to the game on every update tick.
137: 
138:     paddle_velocity : float  [-1.0 … +1.0]
139:         Negative = move left, positive = move right, 0 = stationary.
140:         Magnitude encodes speed (gentle tilt → slow, extreme tilt → fast).
141: 
142:     launch : bool
143:         True for exactly one frame when a LAUNCH flick is detected.
144: 
145:     spin : float  [-1.0 … +1.0]
146:         Wrist rotation mapped to ball spin hint.
147:         Negative = curve left, positive = curve right.
148: 
149:     tilt_y : float  [-1.0 … +1.0]
150:         Forward/back tilt (ay axis relative to calibrated neutral).
151:         Negative = wrist tilted forward (→ UP in Snake).
152:         Positive = wrist tilted back    (→ DOWN in Snake).
153: 
154:     raw_ax : float  — tilt value relative to calibrated neutral (for debug HUD)
155:     raw_gz : float  — smoothed gyroscope Z (for debug HUD)
156:     calibrated : bool  — False while collecting calibration samples
157: 
158:     abs_ax : float  — smoothed absolute accelerometer ax (g) — for calibration view
159:     abs_ay : float  — smoothed absolute accelerometer ay (g)
160:     abs_az : float  — smoothed absolute accelerometer az (g)
161:     abs_gx : float  — raw gyro gx (°/s)
162:     abs_gy : float  — raw gyro gy (°/s)
163:     abs_gz : float  — raw gyro gz (°/s)
164: 
165:     Sensor Fusion (Madgwick AHRS):
166:     qw, qx, qy, qz : float  — quaternion representing orientation
167:     euler_roll : float  — degrees, rotation around x-axis (stable via gravity)
168:     euler_pitch : float  — degrees, rotation around y-axis (stable via gravity)
169:     euler_yaw : float  — degrees, rotation around z-axis (drifts without magnetometer)
170:     av_magnitude : float  — total angular velocity magnitude (°/s)
171: 
172:     Slice Gesture Detection:
173:     slice_active : bool  — True if a slice gesture was detected this frame
174:     slice_direction : str  — direction of slice ("left"/"right"/"up"/"down"/"diagonal_*")
175:     combo_count : int  — number of slices detected within the last 1.5 seconds
176: 
177:     Flick-to-steer (for Snake):
178:     steer_left : bool  — True for one frame on a leftward flick
179:     steer_right : bool — True for one frame on a rightward flick
180:     steer_up : bool    — True for one frame on a forward flick
181:     steer_down : bool  — True for one frame on a backward flick
182:     """
183:     paddle_velocity: float = 0.0
184:     launch: bool = False
185:     spin: float = 0.0
186:     tilt_y: float = 0.0
187:     raw_ax: float = 0.0
188:     raw_gz: float = 0.0
189:     calibrated: bool = False
190:     # Absolute IMU values for calibration visualizer
191:     abs_ax: float = 0.0
192:     abs_ay: float = 0.0
193:     abs_az: float = 0.0
194:     abs_gx: float = 0.0
195:     abs_gy: float = 0.0
196:     abs_gz: float = 0.0
197:     # Sensor fusion (Madgwick filter)
198:     qw: float = 1.0
199:     qx: float = 0.0
200:     qy: float = 0.0
201:     qz: float = 0.0
202:     euler_roll: float = 0.0
203:     euler_pitch: float = 0.0
204:     euler_yaw: float = 0.0
205:     av_magnitude: float = 0.0
206:     # Slice detection
207:     slice_active: bool = False
208:     slice_direction: str = ""
209:     combo_count: int = 0
210:     # Flick-to-steer outputs
211:     steer_left: bool = False
212:     steer_right: bool = False
213:     steer_up: bool = False
214:     steer_down: bool = False
215:     # Functional calibration
216:     functional_calibrating: bool = False
217:     # BMM150 magnetometer calibration state (0 = offline … 3 = fully calibrated)
218:     mag_cal_state: int = 0
219:     # Bosch Kalman Filter hardware outputs (drift-free when hw_fusion_valid=True)
220:     hw_heading: float = 0.0        # compass heading 0-360° (absolute, drift-free yaw)
221:     hw_fusion_valid: bool = False  # True once hardware fusion data is arriving
222:     # True after ~3 s of no samples — games can show a "sensor disconnected" overlay
223:     sensor_disconnected: bool = False

226: # ── Main interpreter ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
227: 
228: class GestureInterpreter:
229:     """
230:     Runs in its own thread, draining the sensor queue and maintaining
231:     the latest GestureState.  The game reads `interpreter.state` each frame.
232: 
233:     Calibration happens automatically during the first ~1 s: hold the sensor
234:     in the neutral (rest) wrist position while the LED is first turning green.
235:     """
236: 
237:     def __init__(
238:         self,
239:         sensor_queue: queue.Queue,
240:         config: Optional[GestureConfig] = None,
241:         sensor=None,
242:     ):
243:         self._q        = sensor_queue
244:         self.config    = config or GestureConfig()
245:         self.state     = GestureState()
246:         self.sensor    = sensor
247:         self._lock     = threading.Lock()
248: 
249:         # Gravity-extraction low-pass filter — all 3 axes
250:         self._smooth_ax: float = 0.0
251:         self._smooth_ay: float = 0.0
252:         self._smooth_az: float = 0.0
253:         self._smooth_gz: float = 0.0
254: 
255:         # Calibrated neutral gravity vector
256:         self._cal_ax: float = 0.0
257:         self._cal_ay: float = 0.0
258:         self._cal_az: float = 0.0
259:         self._calibrated: bool = False
260:         # Accumulation buffer for calibration samples (capped to prevent unbounded growth)
261:         self._cal_buf: deque = deque(maxlen=2 * self.config.calibration_samples)
262: 
263:         self._functional_calibrating: bool = False
264:         self._functional_cal_buf: List[Tuple[float, float]] = []
265: 
266:         # Rolling window for flick detection (stores recent gy samples)
267:         self._gy_window: deque = deque(maxlen=self.config.flick_window) # For launch
268:         # Windows for flick-to-steer
269:         self._gx_steer_window: deque = deque(maxlen=self.config.flick_steer_window)
270:         self._gy_steer_window: deque = deque(maxlen=self.config.flick_steer_window)
271: 
272: 
273:         self._last_steer_time: float = 0.0
274:         self._last_launch_time: float = 0.0
275:         self._running = False
276:         self._thread: Optional[threading.Thread] = None
277:         self._sample_count: int = 0
278:         # Disconnect detection: track time of last received sample
279:         self._last_sample_time: float = 0.0
280:         self._disconnect_reported: bool = False
281: 
282:         # Optional sensor reference for mag calibration polling
283:         self._sensor = sensor
284:         self._mag_cal_poll_next: float = 0.0
285: 
286:         # Sensor fusion and slice detection
287:         self._fusion: FusionProcessor = FusionProcessor()
288:         self._slice: SliceDetector = SliceDetector()
289:         self._last_ts: float = 0.0
290: 
291:     # ── Lifecycle ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
292: 
293:     def start(self) -> None:
294:         self._running = True
295:         self._thread  = threading.Thread(
296:             target=self._loop, daemon=True, name="gesture-interp"
297:         )
298:         self._thread.start()
299: 
300:     def stop(self) -> None:
301:         self._running = False
302:         if self._thread:
303:             self._thread.join(timeout=2)
304: 
305:     def vibrate(self, duration: float = 0.15) -> None:
306:         """Trigger haptic buzz on the sensor (no-op if no sensor attached)."""
307:         if self._sensor is not None:
308:             self._sensor.vibrate(duration)
309: 
310:     def save_calibration_to_nvm(self) -> None:
311:         """Persist current magnetometer calibration offsets to sensor NVM."""
312:         if self._sensor is not None:
313:             self._sensor.save_calibration_to_nvm()
314: 
315:     def recalibrate(self) -> None:
316:         """Force a new calibration cycle (call when sensor position changes)."""
317:         with self._lock:
318:             self._calibrated = False
319:             self._cal_buf.clear()
320:             self.state.calibrated = False
321:         logger.info("Recalibration started — hold sensor still…")
322: 
323:     def start_functional_calibration(self) -> None:
324:         """Triggers a functional_cal_seconds window to learn the natural swing axis."""
325:         with self._lock:
326:             self._functional_calibrating = True
327:             self._functional_cal_buf.clear()
328:         logger.info("Functional calibration started — swing left and right…")
329: 
330:     def align_functional_axis(self, tilt_samples: List[Tuple[float, float]]) -> None:
331:         """
332:         Phase 4: Medical-Grade Functional Calibration (PCA).
333:         Takes a list of raw (tilt_x, tilt_y) points from a natural arm motion,
334:         finds the primary axis of motion, and rotates the coordinates to match it.
335:         """
336:         n = len(tilt_samples)
337:         if n < 10:
338:             return
339:             
340:         mean_x = sum(v[0] for v in tilt_samples) / n
341:         mean_y = sum(v[1] for v in tilt_samples) / n
342:         
343:         cxx = sum((v[0] - mean_x)**2 for v in tilt_samples)
344:         cxy = sum((v[0] - mean_x)*(v[1] - mean_y) for v in tilt_samples)
345:         cyy = sum((v[1] - mean_y)**2 for v in tilt_samples)
346:         
347:         if cxx == cyy and cxy == 0:
348:             return
349:             
350:         angle = 0.5 * math.atan2(2 * cxy, cxx - cyy)
351:         with self._lock:
352:             self.config.yaw_offset_rads = angle
353:         logger.info("PCA Functional Calibration: Rotated axes by %.1f°", math.degrees(angle))
354: 
355:     def get_state(self) -> GestureState:
356:         """Thread-safe snapshot of the latest gesture state."""
357:         with self._lock:
358:             return replace(self.state)
359: 
360:     # ── Processing loop ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
361: 
362:     def _loop(self) -> None:
363:         while self._running:
364:             try:
365:                 sample: IMUSample = self._q.get(timeout=0.05)
366:             except queue.Empty:
367:                 # No new data — decay velocity toward zero to prevent drift
368:                 with self._lock:
369:                     self.state.paddle_velocity *= 0.85
370:                     self.state.launch = False
371:                     self.state.steer_left = False
372:                     self.state.steer_right = False
373:                     self.state.steer_up = False
374:                     self.state.steer_down = False
375:                     # Disconnect detection: report after 3 s of silence
376:                     if (self._last_sample_time > 0
377:                             and time.monotonic() - self._last_sample_time > 3.0
378:                             and not self._disconnect_reported):
379:                         self.state.sensor_disconnected = True
380:                         self._disconnect_reported = True
381:                         logger.warning("No sensor data for 3 s — sensor may be disconnected")
382:                 continue
383:             self._last_sample_time = time.monotonic()
384:             if self._disconnect_reported:
385:                 with self._lock:
386:                     self.state.sensor_disconnected = False
387:                 self._disconnect_reported = False
388:                 logger.info("Sensor data resumed")
389:             self._process(sample)
390: 
391:     def _process(self, s: IMUSample) -> None:
392:         cfg = self.config
393:         a   = cfg.alpha
394: 
395:         # ── Gravity-extraction low-pass filter (all 3 axes) ────────────────
396:         # Low alpha (0.05) means only very slow changes pass through —
397:         # exactly what we want: gravity is DC, motion acceleration is AC.
398:         self._smooth_ax = a * s.ax + (1 - a) * self._smooth_ax
399:         self._smooth_ay = a * s.ay + (1 - a) * self._smooth_ay
400:         self._smooth_az = a * s.az + (1 - a) * self._smooth_az
401:         self._smooth_gz = a * s.gz + (1 - a) * self._smooth_gz
402: 
403:         # ── Medical-Grade Adaptive Baseline (Washout Filter) ───────────────
404:         # Instead of a strict 1-second static calibration, we continuously
405:         # drag the baseline toward the current position VERY slowly.
406:         # This accommodates children who cannot hold still, and adapts if
407:         # their resting posture changes due to fatigue or spasticity.
408:         if not self._calibrated:
409:             self._cal_buf.append((self._smooth_ax, self._smooth_ay, self._smooth_az))
410:             if len(self._cal_buf) >= cfg.calibration_samples:
411:                 # Use median instead of mean to ignore large tremor spikes
412:                 sorted_ax = sorted(v[0] for v in self._cal_buf)
413:                 sorted_ay = sorted(v[1] for v in self._cal_buf)
414:                 sorted_az = sorted(v[2] for v in self._cal_buf)
415:                 
416:                 n = len(self._cal_buf)
417:                 self._cal_ax = sorted_ax[n // 2]
418:                 self._cal_ay = sorted_ay[n // 2]
419:                 self._cal_az = sorted_az[n // 2]
420:                 self._calibrated = True
421:                 self._cal_buf.clear()
422:                 logger.info(
423:                     "Calibrated — neutral gravity: ax=%+.3f  ay=%+.3f  az=%+.3f g",
424:                     self._cal_ax, self._cal_ay, self._cal_az
425:                 )
426:             with self._lock:
427:                 self.state.paddle_velocity = 0.0
428:                 self.state.launch = False
429:                 self.state.calibrated = False
430:             return
431:         else:
432:             # Continuous adaptation: if they are relatively still (not actively
433:             # swiping), slowly pull the baseline to their current resting state.
434:             gyro_mag = math.sqrt(s.gx**2 + s.gy**2 + s.gz**2)
435:             if gyro_mag < cfg.gyro_adapt_threshold:  # Allow for tremors, but ignore big swipes
436:                 # adapt_rate at 100 Hz ≈ 5 s to fully adapt to a new resting posture.
437:                 ar = cfg.adapt_rate
438:                 self._cal_ax = ar * self._smooth_ax + (1 - ar) * self._cal_ax
439:                 self._cal_ay = ar * self._smooth_ay + (1 - ar) * self._cal_ay
440:                 self._cal_az = ar * self._smooth_az + (1 - ar) * self._cal_az
441: 
442:         # ── Tilt from gravity vector relative to calibrated neutral ────────
443:         # When the wrist tilts sideways, lateral gravity (ax) increases while
444:         # vertical gravity (az) decreases.  Subtracting the neutral ax gives
445:         # the pure tilt component, independent of sensor mounting orientation.
446:         raw_tilt_x = self._smooth_ax - self._cal_ax
447:         raw_tilt_y = self._smooth_ay - self._cal_ay
448:         
449:         # Phase 4: Functional Calibration data collection
450:         if self._functional_calibrating:
451:             self._functional_cal_buf.append((raw_tilt_x, raw_tilt_y))
452:             cal_target = int(cfg.functional_cal_seconds * 100)  # samples @ ~100 Hz
453:             if len(self._functional_cal_buf) >= cal_target:
454:                 self.align_functional_axis(self._functional_cal_buf)
455:                 with self._lock:
456:                     self._functional_calibrating = False
457:                     self.state.functional_calibrating = False
458:             else:
459:                 with self._lock:
460:                     self.state.functional_calibrating = True
461: 
462:         # Phase 4: Apply functional alignment rotation (PCA)
463:         # This aligns the physical motion axis with the game's X/Y axis
464:         cos_off = math.cos(cfg.yaw_offset_rads)
465:         sin_off = math.sin(cfg.yaw_offset_rads)
466:         
467:         tilt = raw_tilt_x * cos_off + raw_tilt_y * sin_off
468:         aligned_tilt_y = -raw_tilt_x * sin_off + raw_tilt_y * cos_off
469: 
470:         thr   = cfg.tilt_threshold
471:         t_max = cfg.tilt_max
472: 
473:         if abs(tilt) < thr:
474:             velocity = 0.0
475:         else:
476:             # Map [thr … t_max] → [0 … 1], clamp at 1
477:             magnitude = (abs(tilt) - thr) / max(t_max - thr, 1e-6)
478:             magnitude = min(magnitude, 1.0)
479:             velocity  = magnitude if tilt > 0 else -magnitude
480: 
481:         # ── Forward/back tilt (ay axis) for Snake up/down control ─────────
482:         tilt_y_raw = aligned_tilt_y
483:         if abs(tilt_y_raw) < thr:
484:             tilt_y = 0.0
485:         else:
486:             magnitude_y = (abs(tilt_y_raw) - thr) / max(t_max - thr, 1e-6)
487:             magnitude_y = min(magnitude_y, 1.0)
488:             tilt_y = magnitude_y if tilt_y_raw > 0 else -magnitude_y
489: 
490:         # ── Flick detection for LAUNCH ─────────────────────────────────────
491:         # Sharp spike in gy (pitch axis) = flick upward.
492:         self._gy_window.append(s.gy)
493:         launch = False
494:         if len(self._gy_window) == cfg.flick_window:
495:             peak = max(abs(v) for v in self._gy_window)
496:             now  = time.monotonic()
497:             if (
498:                 peak > cfg.flick_threshold
499:                 and now - self._last_launch_time > cfg.launch_cooldown
500:             ):
501:                 launch = True
502:                 self._last_launch_time = now
503: 
504:         # ── Flick-to-steer detection (Snake) ───────────────────────────────
505:         # Sharp spike in gx (roll axis) = left/right flick.
506:         # Sharp spike in gy (pitch axis) = forward/back flick.
507:         steer_left = steer_right = steer_up = steer_down = False
508:         if cfg.flick_steer_enabled:
509:             self._gx_steer_window.append(s.gx)
510:             self._gy_steer_window.append(s.gy)
511:             now = time.monotonic()
512:             if now - self._last_steer_time > cfg.flick_steer_cooldown:
513:                 # Check X-axis (roll) for left/right steering
514:                 if len(self._gx_steer_window) == cfg.flick_steer_window:
515:                     gx_peak = max(self._gx_steer_window, key=abs)
516:                     if abs(gx_peak) > cfg.flick_steer_threshold:
517:                         if gx_peak > 0:
518:                             steer_right = True
519:                         else:
520:                             steer_left = True
521:                         self._last_steer_time = now
522: 
523:                 # Check Y-axis (pitch) for up/down steering (if no X-flick)
524:                 if not (steer_left or steer_right):
525:                     if len(self._gy_steer_window) == cfg.flick_steer_window:
526:                         gy_peak = max(self._gy_steer_window, key=abs)
527:                         if abs(gy_peak) > cfg.flick_steer_threshold:
528:                             # Pitch forward (nose down) = negative gy
529:                             if gy_peak < 0:
530:                                 steer_up = True
531:                             else:
532:                                 steer_down = True
533:                             self._last_steer_time = now
534: 
535:         # Reset launch flag after one frame
536:         if self.state.launch:
537:             launch = False
538: 
539:         # ── Spin from wrist twist (gz) ─────────────────────────────────────
540:         gz   = self._smooth_gz
541:         dead = cfg.twist_dead_zone
542:         if abs(gz) < dead:
543:             spin = 0.0
544:         else:
545:             spin = (gz - dead) / 200.0 if gz > 0 else (gz + dead) / 200.0
546:             spin = max(-1.0, min(1.0, spin))
547: 
548:         # ── Sensor fusion & slice detection ──────────────────────────────
549:         now_ts = s.timestamp
550:         dt_fusion = (now_ts - self._last_ts) if self._last_ts > 0 else 0.01
551:         self._last_ts = now_ts
552: 
553:         fusion_state = self._fusion.process(s, dt_fusion)

44: W, H           = 800, 600
45: FPS            = 60
46: CELL           = 20
47: COLS           = W // CELL   # 40
48: ROWS           = H // CELL   # 30
49: MOVE_INTERVAL  = 0.12        # seconds per grid step (base)
50: MIN_INTERVAL   = 0.05        # fastest possible
51: TILT_THRESH    = 0.35        # gesture threshold to register a direction change
52: 
53: # Veera mode speed progression (score-based, not per-food)
54: VEERA_GOAL_SCORE         = 200   # reach full speed at this score (20 foods × 10 pts)
55: VEERA_MOVE_INTERVAL_SLOW = 0.28  # very slow start (~3.6 steps/s)
56: VEERA_MOVE_INTERVAL_FULL = 0.07  # full speed (~14.3 steps/s)
57: 
58: # Accessible mode
59: MOVE_INTERVAL_ACCESSIBLE = 0.50   # slower, fixed speed (no acceleration) — half of standard
60: ACCESSIBLE_GESTURE_CD    = 0.8    # seconds between gesture triggers per axis
61: 
62: # ── Colours ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
63: BG          = (15,  15,  25)
64: GRID_CLR    = (38,  38,  60)
65: SNAKE_CLR   = (100, 240, 120)
66: SNAKE_HEAD  = (185, 255, 195)
67: FOOD_CLR    = (255, 100, 100)  # fallback (unused when fruits are drawn)
68: TEXT_CLR    = (255, 255, 255)
69: DIM_CLR     = (165, 165, 180)
70: 
71: FRUITS      = ["apple", "orange", "cherry", "strawberry", "grapes", "watermelon", "lemon"]
72: 
73: 
74: # ── Direction enum ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
75: 
76: class Dir(Enum):
77:     UP    = (0, -1)
78:     DOWN  = (0,  1)
79:     LEFT  = (-1, 0)
80:     RIGHT = (1,  0)
81: 
82:     def opposite(self) -> "Dir":
83:         return {
84:             Dir.UP:    Dir.DOWN,
85:             Dir.DOWN:  Dir.UP,
86:             Dir.LEFT:  Dir.RIGHT,
87:             Dir.RIGHT: Dir.LEFT,
88:         }[self]
